arXiv:2608.02073v1 [math.OC] 03 Aug 2026

Accelerating Evolutionary Strategy via Rao-Blackwellizing Realization of Uncertain Input

So Nakashima ††thanks: naaso0510@gmail.com Affiliation: Institute of Industrial Science Affiliation: The University of Tokyo    Tetsuya J. Kobayashi ††thanks: tetsuya@mail.crmind.net Affiliation: Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo Affiliation: Universal Biology Institute, The University of Tokyo
Abstract

We investigate Optimization under Input Uncertainty (OIU), in which the input to the objective function, rather than the objective function itself, is subject to uncertainty. OIU appears in manufacturing processes with production tolerance, control of physical systems with actuation noise, Mixture of Experts, and Reinforcement Learning (RL). Most of the existing approaches solve OIU by using the value of the objective function but discard the information of the realized input, even though the realized input is observable in various applications. The question here is whether the discarded information of the realized input is useful to accelerate the optimization process. We affirmatively answer this question for Evolutionary Strategy (ES) by theoretically showing that the information of the realized input can reduce the variance of the gradient estimator via Rao-Blackwellization. Using the Rao-Blackwellized gradient estimator, we propose Phenotype-Accelerated Evolutionary Strategy (PAES), which is a refinement of ES for OIU. Numerical experiments show that PAES converges faster than the usual ES from simple continuous optimization problems to RL benchmarks.

   

A Preprint

Keywords evolutionary strategy ⋅\cdot optimization under input uncertainty ⋅\cdot Rao-Blackwellization ⋅\cdot variance reduction ⋅\cdot reinforcement learning

1 Introduction

In this paper, we investigate a class of stochastic optimization problems in which the input to the objective function, rather than to the objective function itself, is subject to uncertainty. Concretely, we specify an input distribution pθ​(x)p_{\theta}(x) of the input xx parameterized by θ\theta and then observe the realization xx of the input and its evaluation f⁡(x)f(x). Our aim is to find the optimal parameter θ\theta of the input distribution that maximizes

F⁡(θ):=𝔼pθ​(x)​[f⁡(x)],\displaystyle F(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{f(x)}\right], (1.1)

the expected value of the evaluation. We call this problem Optimization under Input Uncertainty (OIU) (Figure 1.1).

The uncertainty of input in optimization problems can be found in various contexts [4; 22], such as the manufacturing process with production tolerance [4; 49; 8], the control of robots and spacecraft with actuation noise [12; 37], and performative prediction in machine learning, where the distribution of data depends on the model parameters [38]. While these examples regard randomness in xx as an externally imposed nuisance, the same setup also appears when an algorithm designer intentionally introduces randomness. In addition, we sometimes employ a distribution pθ​(x)p_{\theta}(x) when xx is discrete to make 𝔼pθ​(x)​[f​(x)]\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{f(x)}\right] differentiable with respect to θ\theta. Mixture of Experts (MoE) [23] and classification problems are representative examples. Another important class of problems is Reinforcement Learning (RL) [48], where we introduce stochasticity to a policy to encourage exploration for finding better actions. We also note that a similar structure appears in prompt engineering, since the outputs of Large Language Models (LLMs) are stochastic.

Since a variety of important real-world problems are categorized into this class of problems, several algorithms have been proposed to deal with the uncertainty of the input. An approach is gradient-based algorithms, which minimize the worst-case objective value by assuming boundedness of uncertainty [3; 21; 20]. The second class is Bayesian optimization [12; 36], which constructs a prior distribution of the objective function by incorporating the uncertainty of the input and then updates the distribution by observing the realized input and its evaluation. Yet another approach, which we focus mainly on in this paper, is population-based optimization [5], such as Evolutionary Strategy (ES) [41] and genetic algorithms [51]. ES has demonstrated its efficiency and superiority in RL [44; 30] in terms of scalability and robustness to local optima compared to single-agent RL algorithms [27; 9] (See Appendix A for more detail).

While these algorithms search for an optimal θ\theta using f⁡(x)f(x) of the realized input xx as a feedback signal, they do not utilize the information of the realized input xx itself. Since the realized input xx is observable in many applications, the information it carries could be used to further improve the efficiency of the algorithms. In the manufacturing process, for example, the production tolerance prevents us from completely controlling the resulting product xx, but the manufactured product xx can be measured and therefore observable. Likewise, in the control of physical systems, actuation noise hinders us from completely controlling the trajectory of the system, but we can measure the trajectory afterwards. In particular, ES applied to RL [44] uses only the reward of the episode without tapping into the trajectory of states and actions.

These examples raise a question: is the observation of the input useful for accelerating the optimization? Motivated by the analogy with evolutionary biology, we introduce the Phenotype-Accelerated Evolutionary Strategy (PAES) which achieves the acceleration of ES. In the context of evolutionary biology, the function f⁡(x)f(x) is fitness, which is determined by the phenotypic state xx of an individual (Figure 1.1). The phenotype xx is stochastically determined by the genotype θ\theta as pθ​(x)p_{\theta}(x). Thus, the objective function F⁡(θ)F(\theta) is the fitness of a population with genotype θ\theta. Following the idea of accelerating evolution by learning at the phenotypic level [32; 34], PAES takes advantage of the phenotypic information to design a population-based efficient gradient estimator. Furthermore, we affirmatively and theoretically answer the question by showing that this acceleration is Rao-Blackwellization [40; 6; 28]. Rao-Blackwellization is a technique to reduce the variance of estimation in which we eliminate the randomness from irrelevant random variables by taking a conditional expectation (See Appendix A). PAES replaces the gradient estimation of ES for OIU with its Rao-Blackwellization.

The contribution of this paper is summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a general framework for optimization under input uncertainty (OIU).

  • •

    We show theoretically that observing the realized input can accelerate ES for OIU through Rao–Blackwellization, and we call the resulting accelerated method PAES.

  • •

    For a class of problems, we derive the Rao–Blackwellized gradient estimator analytically and provide a reparameterization-trick approximation to it [25; 42].

  • •

    We demonstrate numerically that PAES converges faster than ES across benchmarks, from simple optimization problems to more complex RL tasks.

We note that a Rao-Blackwellization of a gradient estimator is employed in  [26]. Yet, this work differs from ours in that they take a conditional expectation of the latent variable with respect to the activation of hidden layer whereas we take a conditional expectation of parameters with respect to the realized input.

1.1 Organization of the Paper

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we explain notation and preliminaries. In Section 3, we formulate OIU and outline some examples of OIU. In Section 4, we introduce PAES and show that the variance of the gradient estimator of PAES is smaller than that of ES via Rao-Blackwellization. We also give an analytical form of the gradient estimator of PAES for some specific cases and device an approximation of the gradient estimator via the reparameterization trick. In Section 5 and Section 6, we demonstrate PAES with some examples and conduct the numerical experiments of PAES, respectively. In Section 7, we conclude the paper. Appendix contains the omitted proofs from the main text and additional experimental results.

2 Preliminaries

Before introducing PAES, we clarify the notation to be used and outline the basis of ES and its variants.

2.1 Notation

For a positive integer nn, let [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. For simplicity, we sometimes denote summation ∑i=1Nf⁡(xi)\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(x_{i}) as ∫f⁡(x)​𝑑x\int f(x)\mathrm{d}x. We denote the Kronecker delta function as δx,x′\delta_{x,x^{\prime}}. For a vector 𝒙=(x1,x2,…,xn)\bm{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}), its diagonalization diag⁡(𝒙)\mathrm{diag}(\bm{x}) is defined as the diagonal matrix with x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} on its diagonal.

2.2 Random Variables and Probability Distributions

When a random variable xx follows a certain distribution whose probability density function is p⁡(x)p(x), we write x∼p⁡(x)x\sim p(x). 𝔼p⁡(x)​[f​(x)]\mathbb{E}_{p(x)}\left[{f(x)}\right] denotes the expectation of f⁡(x)f(x) with respect to p⁡(x)p(x). For a random vector v∼p⁡(v)v\sim p(v), we define the variance of vv as 𝕍p⁡(v)​[v]=𝔼p⁡(v)​[‖v‖2]\mathbb{V}_{p(v)}\left[v\right]=\mathbb{E}_{p(v)}\left[{\|v\|^{2}}\right].

For a nn-dimensional normal distribution, we denote its probability density function by N⁡(x∣μ,Σ)N\left({x}\mid{\mu},{\Sigma}\right), where x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is a random variable, μ∈ℝn\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the mean vector, and Σ∈ℝn×n\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is the covariance matrix. Similarly, for a Dirichlet distribution, we denote its probability density function by Dir⁡(π∣α)\mathrm{Dir}(\pi\mid\alpha):

Dir⁡(π∣α)\displaystyle\mathrm{Dir}(\pi\mid\alpha) :=1ℬ⁡(α)​∏i∈[n]πiαi−1,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\mathcal{B}(\alpha)}\prod_{i\in[n]}\pi_{i}^{\alpha_{i}-1}, (2.1)

where π\pi is a probability distribution on [n][n] and and α∈ℝ>0n\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} is the parameter. Here, ℬ⁡(α)\mathcal{B}(\alpha) is the extended Beta function defined by

ℬ⁡(α):=∏i∈[n]Γ⁡(αi)Γ⁡(∑i∈[n]αi),\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\alpha):=\frac{\prod_{i\in[n]}\Gamma(\alpha_{i})}{\Gamma\left(\sum_{i\in[n]}\alpha_{i}\right)}, (2.2)

where Γ⁡(x)\Gamma(x) is the Gamma function.

2.3 Evolutionary Strategy

Given an unconstrained maximization problem of an objective function F:Θ→ℝF\colon\Theta\to\mathbb{R}, where Θ⊆ℝn\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is a search space and its element is typically represented by θ\theta, ES solves the problem by introducing a population, which is written as a distribution qψq_{\psi} on Θ\Theta parameterized by ψ\psi. Instead of directly optimizing F⁡(θ)F(\theta), ES seeks a parameter ψ\psi that maximizes the expected value of F⁡(θ)F(\theta) with respect to qψ​(θ)q_{\psi}(\theta) [41]:

ℱ⁡(ψ):=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[F⁡(θ)].\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\psi):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{F(\theta)}\right]. (2.3)

This expected value is maximized by a stochastic gradient ascent method:

ψt+1=ψt+η​∂ℱ∂ψ¯,\displaystyle\psi_{t+1}=\psi_{t}+\eta\overline{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\psi}}, (2.4)

where ∂ℱ∂ψ¯\overline{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\psi}} is an estimator of ∂ℱ∂ψ\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\psi} and η\eta is a learning rate. By applying the log-derivative trick, the gradient is calculated without computing ∂F⁡(θ)/∂θ\partial F(\theta)/\partial\theta as follows

∂ℱ∂ψ=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[F⁡(θ)​∂log⁡qψ​(θ)∂ψ].\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\psi}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{F(\theta)\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta)}{\partial\psi}}\right]. (2.5)

From this equation, we can estimate the gradient using samples θi∼qψ\theta_{i}\sim q_{\psi} for i∈[N]i\in[N]:

∂ℱ∂ψ≈1N​∑i=1NF⁡(θi)​∂log⁡qψ​(θi)∂ψ=:∂ℱ∂ψ¯.\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\psi}\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{F(\theta_{i})}\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta_{i})}{\partial\psi}=:\overline{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\psi}}. (2.6)

2.4 Modifications and Refinements of ES

The gradient estimator of ES (2.5) is sensitive to the scale of the objective function F⁡(θ)F(\theta), which may worsen the performance of ES in some cases. To address this issue, we can introduce a transformation function W{F⁡(θi)}i:ℝ→ℝW_{\{F(\theta_{i})\}_{i}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, which can depend on a set of evaluations {F⁡(θi)}i\{F(\theta_{i})\}_{i} over the populations. We define a transformed objective function by

ℱW​(ψ):=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[W⁡(F⁡(θ))],\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{W}(\psi):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{W(F(\theta))}\right], (2.7)

and the associated gradient estimator from samples [37];

∂ℱW∂ψ≈1N​∑i=1NW⁡(F⁡(θi))​∂log⁡qψ​(θi)∂ψ,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{W(F(\theta_{i}))}\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta_{i})}{\partial\psi}, (2.8)

where we omit the subscript of W{F⁡(θi)}iW_{\{F(\theta_{i})\}_{i}} for notational simplicity. We can further improve the performance of ES by introducing a natural gradient estimator. Using the Fisher information matrix

ℐ⁡[qψ​(θ)]:=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[∂log⁡qψ​(θ)∂ψ​∂log⁡qψ​(θ)∂ψ⊤],\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\right]:=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta)}{\partial\psi}\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta)}{\partial\psi}^{\top}}\right], (2.9)

the natural gradient is obtained;

∇ℱW​(ψ)=ℐ​[qψ​(θ)]−1​𝔼qψ​(θ)​[W⁡(F⁡(θ))​∂log⁡qψ​(θ)∂ψ],\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{F}_{W}(\psi)=\mathcal{I}\left[{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\right]^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{W(F(\theta))\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta)}{\partial\psi}}\right], (2.10)

where and hereafter ∇\nabla instead of ∂/∂ϕ\partial/\partial\phi is used to indicate the natural gradient. We can approximate the natural gradient by samples in a similar way to (2.8). This method is known as Information Geometric Optimization [37]. The algorithm with transformation function WW is summarized in Algorithm 1.

There exist other finer modifications of the gradient estimator (2.8). The two-point gradient estimator [47; 11; 35; 10] is a major example, and its theoretical analysis shows the superiority of the two-point estimator over the one-point gradient estimator (2.8). The two-point gradient estimator for general ES is defined as follows:

∂ℱW∂ψ¯:=1N​∑i=1N[W⁡(F⁡(θ1i))−W⁡(F⁡(θ2i))2​σ]​[∂log⁡qψ​(θ1i)∂ψ−∂log⁡qψ​(θ2i)∂ψ].\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\frac{W(F(\theta^{i}_{1}))-W(F(\theta^{i}_{2}))}{2\sigma}\right]\left[\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta^{i}_{1})}{\partial\psi}-\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta^{i}_{2})}{\partial\psi}\right]. (2.11)

2.5 Zeroth-Order Optimization: an instance of ES

One of the most popular versions of ES is the case in which the population qψ​(θ)q_{\psi}(\theta) is a Gaussian distribution N⁡(θ∣θ¯,σ2​𝐈)N\left({\theta}\mid{\bar{\theta}},{\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}}\right) with σ\sigma as a hyperparameter. In this case, the gradient of ℱW\mathcal{F}_{W} in (2.8) is reduced to the following form:

∂ℱW∂ψ≈1N​σ​∑i=1NW⁡(F⁡(θi))​ϵi,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}\approx\frac{1}{N\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{W(F(\theta_{i}))}\epsilon_{i}, (2.12)

where ϵi=(θi−θ¯)/σ\epsilon_{i}=(\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta})/\sigma. This method is called Zeroth-Order Optimization (ZOO). The two-point gradient estimator for ZOO becomes

∂ℱW∂ψ¯=1N​σ​∑i=1N[W⁡(F⁡(θ1i))−W⁡(F⁡(θ2i))2​σ]​ϵi.\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}}=\frac{1}{N\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\frac{W(F(\theta^{i}_{1}))-W(F(\theta^{i}_{2}))}{2\sigma}\right]\epsilon_{i}. (2.13)

3 Formalization of Optimization under Input Uncertainty (OIU)

In this section, we formalize OIU. Let 𝒳⊂ℝn\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be an input space (possibly a discrete space), and f:𝒳→ℝf\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be an objective function over the input space. Let Θ⊆ℝm\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} and assume that, for each θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, a probability distribution pθp_{\theta} on 𝒳\mathcal{X} is associated. Our aim is to maximize the following objective function over the search space Θ\Theta:

F⁡(θ):=𝔼pθ​(x)​[f⁡(x)].\displaystyle F(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{f(x)}\right]. (3.1)

In the following, we call pθp_{\theta} the input distribution.

3.1 Examples of OIU

3.1.1 Continuous Optimization with Input Noise

Let us consider the case where we optimize an objective function f:ℝn→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, but the input xx is perturbed by an input noise. Specifically, in each trial, we choose an intended input θi∈ℝn\theta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then, we observe a realized input xix_{i}, which is perturbed by the input noise as xi=θi+ϵix_{i}=\theta_{i}+\epsilon_{i}, where ϵi\epsilon_{i} is the input noise that follows some distribution h⁡(ϵi∣θi)h(\epsilon_{i}\mid\theta_{i}). We then observe the feedback f⁡(xi)f(x_{i}). In this situation, our objective is to maximize the expected value of 𝔼ϵi​[f⁡(θi+ϵi)]\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon_{i}}\left[{f(\theta_{i}+\epsilon_{i})}\right]. By setting pθi​(x)=h⁡(x−θi∣θi)p_{\theta_{i}}(x)=h(x-\theta_{i}\mid\theta_{i}), this problem is formulated within the framework of (3.1).

3.1.2 Reinforcement Learning

In RL, our objective is to find a policy πθ​(a∣s)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s), where aa is an action and ss is a state, which maximizes the expected cumulative reward. The expected cumulative reward is given by

F⁡(θ)=𝔼ℙFθ​[∑t=0∞γt​r​(st,at)],\displaystyle F(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}^{\theta}}\left[{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})}\right], (3.2)

where r⁡(s,a)r(s,a) is a reward function and γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is a discount factor. Here, we define ℙFθ\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}^{\theta} as the law of the trajectory of states and actions produced by a policy πθ​(a∣s)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) and a given transition matrix 𝐓⁡(s′∣s,a)\mathbf{T}(s^{\prime}\mid s,a). The explicit form of ℙFθ\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}^{\theta} is

ℙFθ​(a0,s1,a1,s2,…∣s0)=∏t=0∞πθ​(at∣st)​𝐓​(st+1∣st,at).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}^{\theta}(a_{0},s_{1},a_{1},s_{2},\dots\mid s_{0})=\prod_{t=0}^{\infty}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\mathbf{T}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}). (3.3)

By setting sample x=(a0,s1,a1,s2,…)x=(a_{0},s_{1},a_{1},s_{2},\dots) and pθ=ℙFθp_{\theta}=\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}^{\theta}, we see that this problem is in the framework of (3.1).

3.2 Extension of OIU

We may extend OIU to Contextual Optimization under Input Uncertainty (COIU) where f⁡(x)f(x) and pθ​(x)p_{\theta}(x) are also dependent on a context cc as in f⁡(x,c)f(x,c) and pθ​(x|c)p_{\theta}(x|c). This extension covers a wider range of applications such as mixture of experts and classification with bandit feedback. To keep the main body of the text simple, we discuss this extension in Appendix B.

4 Phenotype-Accelerated Evolutionary Strategy (PAES) for OIU

In this section, we introduce PAES and its core component, the phenotype gradient estimator. As PAES is an extension of ES for OIU, we first illustrate how ES is adopted to solve OIU and how its gradient estimator can be improved by exploiting the realized input xx.

4.1 Evolutionary Strategy for OIU and Genotype Gradient Estimator

Give the objective function F⁡(θ)F(\theta) of OIU, its smoothed version by a distribution qψ​(θ)q_{\psi}(\theta) is obtained as

ℱ⁡(ψ):=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[F⁡(θ)]=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[𝔼pθ​(x)​[f⁡(x)]].\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\psi):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{F(\theta)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{f(x)}\right]}\right]. (4.1)

where qψ​(θ)q_{\psi}(\theta) is interpreted as the diversity of genotypes (Figure 4.1). We can also define a transformed objective function:

ℱW​(ψ):=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[𝔼pθ​(x)​[W⁡(f⁡(x))]].\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{W}(\psi):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{W(f(x))}\right]}\right]. (4.2)

The gradient is calculated via (2.5):

∂ℱW∂ψ=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[𝔼pθ​(x)​[W⁡(f⁡(x))]​∂log⁡qψ​(θ)∂ψ].\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{W(f(x))}\right]\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta)}{\partial\psi}}\right]. (4.3)

Then, we obtain an estimate of this expression by sampling:

Definition 1 (Genotype gradient estimator).
∂∂ψ¯g​ℱW:=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​∂log⁡qψ​(θi)∂ψ.\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal{F}_{W}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{W(f(x_{i}))\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta_{i})}{\partial\psi}}. (4.4)

Since this estimator is obtained by applying ES to the objective function F⁡(θ)F(\theta) with respect to θ\theta, i.e., genotype information, we call it the genotype gradient estimator.

We can also apply ZOO (2.12) to continuous optimization with input noise (Section 3.1.1), for which the genotype gradient estimator is given by

∂ℱW∂ψ≈1N​σ​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​ϵi,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}\approx\frac{1}{N\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{W(f(x_{i}))}\epsilon_{i}, (4.5)

where ϵi=(θi−θ¯)/σ\epsilon_{i}=(\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta})/\sigma.

4.2 Intuition behind Improvement of Gradient by Phenotypic Information

One potential problem of the genotype gradient estimator (4.5) is that it utilizes only the evaluation f⁡(xi)f(x_{i}) and the intended input θi\theta_{i}, i.e., the fitness value and the gennotype information. The information of realized input xix_{i}, i.e., the phenotypic information, is discarded. Let us illustrate that the realized input xix_{i} has richer information than f⁡(xi)f(x_{i}) and θi\theta_{i} for gradient estimation by the following example.

We consider an extreme example under the problem setting in Section 3.1.1, where the population distribution is singular. Concretely, we assume that h⁡(ϵi∣θi)=N⁡(ϵi∣𝟎,𝐈)h(\epsilon_{i}\mid\theta_{i})=N\left({\epsilon_{i}}\mid{\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}}\right), where ϵi=(xi−θi)/σ\epsilon_{i}=(x_{i}-\theta_{i})/\sigma. We also assume that ψ=θ\psi=\theta and qψq_{\psi} is a delta distribution δθ\delta_{\theta}. We further assume that W⁡(f⁡(x))=f⁡(x)W(f(x))=f(x). As a consequence, the genotype gradient estimator (4.5) becomes meaningless since we can no longer define ∂log⁡qψ​(θ)∂ψ\frac{\partial\log q_{\psi}(\theta)}{\partial\psi}. This is because, while the estimator (4.5) uses the diversity of θ\theta for the estimation of the gradient, there is no diversity of θ\theta in this case. However, by following a similar argument to the usual ES, we can estimate the gradient even in this case by using the realized input. As shown in the next section (see Theorem 3), we have

∂ℱW∂ψ=1σ​𝔼pθ​(x)​[f⁡(x)​ϵ]=1σ2​𝔼pθ​(x)​[f⁡(x)​(x−θ)],\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}=\frac{1}{\sigma}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{f(x)\epsilon}\right]=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{f(x)(x-\theta)}\right], (4.6)

where ϵ=(x−θ)/σ\epsilon=(x-\theta)/\sigma. From this equation, we can estimate the gradient as follows:

∂ℱW∂θ≈1N​σ2​∑i=1Nf⁡(xi)​(xi−θ).\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\theta}\approx\frac{1}{N\sigma^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{f(x_{i})(x_{i}-\theta)}. (4.7)

This example illuminates that the realized input xix_{i} is useful for estimating gradient, and we can construct a new gradient estimator (4.6).

4.3 Phenotype gradient estimator and PAES

By generalizing the procedure in the example above, we define another gradient estimator:

Definition 2 (Phenotype gradient estimator).

For a joint distribution ℙF​(x,θ)=pθ​(x)​qψ​(θ)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta)=p_{\theta}(x)q_{\psi}(\theta) and its marginal distribution ℙF​(x)=∫ℙF​(x,θ)​𝑑θ\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)=\int\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta, a gradient estimator is defined as follows:

∂∂ψ¯p​ℱW:=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​∂log⁡ℙF​(xi)∂ψ.\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{W(f(x_{i}))\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x_{i})}{\partial\psi}}. (4.8)

We call this estimator phenotype gradient estimator since it utilizes the diversity of both genotype θ\theta and phenotype xx.

The relationship between the genotype gradient estimator and the phenotype gradient estimator is illustrated in Figure 4.1.

Theorem 3.

The phenotype gradient estimator is an unbiased estimator as the genotype gradient estimator is:

∂ℱW∂ψ=𝔼ℙF​(x)​[W⁡(f⁡(x))​∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ].\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\left[{W(f(x))\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi}}\right]. (4.9)

In addition, the phenotype gradient estimator is superior to the genotype gradient estimator in that it has smaller variance than the genotype gradient estimator:

𝕍ℙF​[∂∂ψ¯p​ℱW]≤𝕍ℙF​[∂∂ψ¯g​ℱW].\displaystyle\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W}\right]\leq\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal{F}_{W}\right]. (4.10)
Proof of Equation (4.9) and Equation (4.6).

We have

∂ℱW∂ψ\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi} =∂∂ψ​∫W⁡(f⁡(x))​ℙF​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}\int W(f(x))\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)\mathrm{d}x (4.11)
=∫W⁡(f⁡(x))​∂ℙF​(x)∂ψ​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int W(f(x))\frac{\partial\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi}\mathrm{d}x (4.12)
=∫[W⁡(f⁡(x))​∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ]​ℙF​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int\left[W(f(x))\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi}\right]\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)\mathrm{d}x (4.13)
=𝔼ℙF​(x)​[W⁡(f⁡(x))​∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\left[{W(f(x))\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi}}\right]. (4.14)

This proves Equation (4.9). Equation (4.6) is the special case of this equation. ∎

The proof of Equation (4.10) is given in Section C.1.

By replacing the genotype gradient estimator in ES for OIU with the phenotype gradient estimator, we introduce Phenotype-Accelerated Evolutionary Strategy (PAES) (Algorithm 2) as follows:

4.4 Phenotype Gradient Estimator as the Rao-Blackwellized Estimator

To systematically extend generalized genotype gradient estimators (e.g., the two-point estimator (2.11)) to their phenotype counterparts, it is crucial to first generalize Theorem 3. Here, we clarify that this generalization is achieved by an argument similar to the Rao-Blackwell theorem.

Recall that, at each generation tt, we sample (θi(t),xi(t))({\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}) from ℙF​(x,θ)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta) independently for i∈[N]i\in[N]. Let us assume that we have some unbiased estimator U⁡({θi(t),xi(t)}i∈[N])U\left({\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right) of the gradient for these samples i∈[N]i\in[N].

Definition 4 (Rao-Blackwellized estimator).

Given an estimator U⁡({θi(t),xi(t)}i∈[N])U\left({\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right), a Rao-Blackwellized estimator RB⁡[U]\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right] is defined by

RB⁡[U]​({xi(t)}i∈[N]):=𝔼ℙF​[{θi(t)}i∈[N]∣{xi(t)}i∈[N]]​[U⁡({θi(t),xi(t)}i∈[N])],\displaystyle\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}[\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}\mid\{{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}]}\left[{U\left({\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right)}\right], (4.15)

where the expectation is taken over ℙF​(θ∣x)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta\mid x) for all pairs of (θi(t),xi(t))({\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}) independently. Here, ℙF​(θ∣x)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta\mid x) is the conditional distribution defined by ℙF​(x,θ)/ℙF​(x)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta)/\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x).

For this Rao-Blackwellized estimator, we can prove a generalization of Theorem 3 .

Theorem 5 (Generalization of Theorem 3).

The Rao-blackwellized estimator is unbiased.

𝔼ℙF​[RB⁡[U]​({xi(t)}i∈[N])]=𝔼ℙF​[U⁡({θi(t),xi(t)}i∈[N])].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{U\left({\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right)}\right]. (4.16)

In addition, the Rao-blackwellized estimator has smaller variance than the original estimator:

𝕍ℙF​[RB⁡[U]​({xi(t)}i∈[N])]≤𝕍ℙF​[U⁡({θi(t),xi(t)}i∈[N])].\displaystyle\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({{\{{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}}\right)\right]\leq\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[U\left({\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right)\right]. (4.17)

The proofs are given in Section C.1. We can check that Theorem 3 is a special case of Rao-Blackwellization by using the following proposition:

Proposition 6 (Phenotype gradient estimator is a Rao-Blackwellized estimator).
RB⁡[∂∂ψ¯g​ℱW]=∂∂ψ¯p​ℱW.\displaystyle\mathrm{RB}\left[{\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal{F}_{W}}\right]=\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W}. (4.18)

The proof is given in Section C.1.

4.5 Analytical Form of Phenotype Gradient Estimator

The phenotype gradient estimator requires the computation of ∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi}. This can be analytically achieved when the input distribution pθp_{\theta} belongs to an exponential family and qψq_{\psi} belongs to its conjugate family.

Suppose that x∈𝒳⊆ℝkx\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{k} and

pθ​(x)=h⁡(x)​exp⁡(θ⋅u⁡(x)−A⁡(θ)),\displaystyle p_{\theta}(x)=h(x)\exp\left(\theta\cdot u(x)-A(\theta)\right), (4.19)

where u⁡(x):𝒳→ℝnu(x)\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} and h:𝒳→ℝh\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} , and A⁡(θ)A(\theta) is a logarithm of the normalization constant defined by

A(θ)=log∫h(x)exp(θ⋅u(x))dx.\displaystyle A(\theta)=\log\int h(x)\exp\left(\theta\cdot u(x)\right)\mathrm{d}x. (4.20)

We also assume that qψq_{\psi} belongs to the conjugate family of pθp_{\theta}:

qψ​(θ)=exp⁡(ν​ϕ⋅θ−ν​A​(θ)−B⁡(ϕ,ν)),\displaystyle q_{\psi}(\theta)=\exp\left(\nu\phi\cdot\theta-\nu A(\theta)-B(\phi,\nu)\right), (4.21)

where ν∈ℝ\nu\in\mathbb{R}, ψ=(ϕ,ν)∈ℝk×ℝ\psi=(\phi,\nu)\in\mathbb{R}^{k}\times\mathbb{R}, and B⁡(ϕ,ν)B(\phi,\nu) is the logarithm of the normalization constant defined by

B(ϕ,ν)=log∫exp(νϕ⋅θ−νA(θ))dθ.\displaystyle B(\phi,\nu)=\log\int\exp\left(\nu\phi\cdot\theta-\nu A(\theta)\right)\mathrm{d}\theta. (4.22)
Proposition 7.

For the exponential family and its conjugate, ∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi} is analytically represented as

∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ϕ=𝔼qψ′​(θ)​[ν′​θ]−𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ν​θ],\displaystyle\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\phi}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi^{\prime}}(\theta)}\left[{\nu^{\prime}\theta}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\nu\theta}\right], (4.23)
∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ν=𝔼qψ′​(θ)​[ϕ′⋅θ−A⁡(θ)]−𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ϕ⋅θ−A⁡(θ)].\displaystyle\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\nu}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi^{\prime}}(\theta)}\left[{\phi^{\prime}\cdot\theta-A(\theta)}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\phi\cdot\theta-A(\theta)}\right]. (4.24)

where ψ′=(ϕ′,ν′)\psi^{\prime}=(\phi^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}) and

ϕ′=ν​ϕ+u⁡(x)ν+1,\displaystyle\phi^{\prime}=\frac{\nu\phi+u(x)}{\nu+1}, (4.25)
ν′=ν+1.\displaystyle\nu^{\prime}=\nu+1. (4.26)

Moreover, if we parameterize qψq_{\psi} by the expectation parameter,

η⁡(ψ)=(𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ν​θ],𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ϕ⋅θ−A⁡(θ)])⊤,\displaystyle\eta(\psi)=(\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\nu\theta}\right],\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\phi\cdot\theta-A(\theta)}\right])^{\top}, (4.27)

the natural gradient is calculated as follows [37]:

∇ηϕ​log​ℙF​(x)=𝔼qψ′​(θ)​[ν′​θ]−𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ν​θ],\displaystyle\nabla_{\eta_{\phi}}\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi^{\prime}}(\theta)}\left[{\nu^{\prime}\theta}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\nu\theta}\right], (4.28)
∇ην​log​ℙF​(x)=𝔼qψ′​(θ)​[ϕ′⋅θ−A⁡(θ)]−𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ϕ⋅θ−A⁡(θ)].\displaystyle\nabla_{\eta_{\nu}}\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi^{\prime}}(\theta)}\left[{\phi^{\prime}\cdot\theta-A(\theta)}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\phi\cdot\theta-A(\theta)}\right]. (4.29)

The proof is given in Section C.2.

4.6 Remark on the Space Where Fisher Information Matrix Is Defined

In equations (4.28), the Fisher information matrix is defined by (2.9). However, we have another choice of the Fisher information matrix based on ℙF\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}:

ℐ⁡[ℙF​(x)]=𝔼ℙF​(x)​[∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ​∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ⊤].\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\left[{\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi}\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi}^{\top}}\right]. (4.30)

For some cases (e.g. Section 5.1), this Fisher information matrix leads to an easier update rule. Let us compare these two definitions of the natural gradient. As discussed in [2], the natural gradient is characterized by the following variational problem. For any distribution pp, we have

ℐ​[p]−1​∂ℱW∂ψ=limϵ→0argmaxδ​p[ℱW​(ψ+δ​p)],\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{p}\right]^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\operatornamewithlimits{argmax}_{\delta p}\left[\mathcal{F}_{W}(\psi+\delta p)\right], (4.31)

where δ​p\delta p satisfies 𝒟KL​(p∣p+δ​p)=ϵ\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\mid p+\delta p)=\epsilon. Thus, the natural gradient is the direction where the objective function increases the most when we measure the "distance" by the KL divergence. Under this interpretation, the natural gradient with ℐ​[qψ​(θ)]\mathcal{I}\left[{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\right] is the direction to which the objective function increases the most when the distance is measured by 𝒟KL​(qψ​(θ)∣qψ+δ​ψ​(θ))\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\psi}(\theta)\mid q_{\psi+\delta\psi}(\theta)). On the other hand, the natural gradient with ℐ​[ℙF​(x)]\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right] is the direction to which the objective function increases the most when the distance is measured by 𝒟KL​(ℙF​(x∣ψ)∣ℙF​(x∣ψ+δ​ψ))\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x\mid\psi)\mid\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x\mid\psi+\delta\psi)). We also note that the Fisher information matrix of ℙF​(x,θ)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta) is the same as that of qψ​(θ)q_{\psi}(\theta):

ℐ⁡[ℙF​(x,θ)]=𝔼ℙF​(x,θ)​[∂log⁡ℙF​(x,θ)∂ψ​∂log⁡ℙF​(x,θ)∂ψ⊤]=ℐ⁡[qψ​(θ)].\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta)}\left[{\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta)}{\partial\psi}\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta)}{\partial\psi}^{\top}}\right]=\mathcal{I}\left[{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\right]. (4.32)

Therefore, we have two options for the distance measure of probability distributions and the corresponding Fisher metric, and we should choose the one that is best suited to the problem under consideration.

4.7 Approximation of Phenotype Gradient Estimator via Reparameterization Trick

Most OIU problems may not fall within the case of Section 4.5. To cover a wider range of problems, approximation methods to calculate the phenotype gradient estimator are crucial. We derive it by the application of the reparameterization trick.

Let us assume that θ\theta is decided deterministically from some noise: θ=βψ​(ξ)\theta=\beta_{\psi}(\xi), where ξ\xi follows a distribution q⁡(ξ)q(\xi) and βψ​(⋅)\beta_{\psi}(\cdot) is a deterministic function. A typical example is Gaussian input noise: ξ∼N⁡(ξ∣𝟎,𝐈)\xi\sim N\left({\xi}\mid{\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}}\right) and βψ​(ξ)=θ¯+σ​ξ\beta_{\psi}(\xi)=\bar{\theta}+\sigma\xi, where ψ=(θ¯,σ)\psi=(\bar{\theta},\sigma). In this setting, the expectation ℱW\mathcal{F}_{W} of the objective function becomes

ℱ⁡(ψ)=𝔼q⁡(ξ)​[𝔼pβψ​(ξ)​(x)​[W⁡(f⁡(x))]].\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\psi)=\mathbb{E}_{q(\xi)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}(x)}\left[{W(f(x))}\right]}\right]. (4.33)

Then, we can calculate the gradient as

∂ℱW∂ψ=𝔼q⁡(ξ)​[∂βψ​(ξ)∂ψ​[∂∂θ​𝔼pθ​(x)​[W⁡(f⁡(x))]]θ=βψ​(ξ)].\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}=\mathbb{E}_{q(\xi)}\left[{\frac{\partial\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}{\partial\psi}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{W(f(x))}\right]\right]_{\theta=\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}}\right]. (4.34)

By applying the log-derivative trick to the inner expectation, we have

∂ℱW∂ψ=𝔼q⁡(ξ)​[∂βψ​(ξ)∂ψ​𝔼pθ​(x)​[W⁡(f⁡(x))​[∂log⁡pθ​(x)∂θ]θ=βψ​(ξ)]].\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{W}}{\partial\psi}=\mathbb{E}_{q(\xi)}\left[{\frac{\partial\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}{\partial\psi}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x)}\left[{W(f(x))\left[\frac{\partial\log p_{\theta}(x)}{\partial\theta}\right]_{\theta=\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}}\right]}\right]. (4.35)

By approximating the right hand side by samples, we have the following gradient estimator:

∂∂ψ¯r​ℱW=1N​∑i=1N∂βψ​(ξi)∂ψ​W​(f⁡(xi))​[∂log⁡pθ​(xi)∂θ]θ=βψ​(ξi).\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{r}}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\partial\beta_{\psi}(\xi_{i})}{\partial\psi}W(f(x_{i}))\left[\frac{\partial\log p_{\theta}(x_{i})}{\partial\theta}\right]_{\theta=\beta_{\psi}(\xi_{i})}. (4.36)

This estimator is not Rao-Blackwellized since it contains irrelevant random variables ξi\xi_{i} on the right hand side, which are not deterministically decided by ψ\psi and xx. However, the dependency on ξ\xi is very weak in some cases. We will see an example in Section 5.3.

5 Phenotype Gradient Estimators for Representative OIU Problems

In this section, we illustrate how the phenotype gradient estimator is obtained for specific OIU problems. For COIU which includes mixture of experts and classification with bandit feedback, see Appendix B.

5.1 OIU with Gaussian Distributions and its Phenotype Gradient Estimator

Let us consider the case where qψq_{\psi} and pθp_{\theta} are Gaussian as in Example 3.1.1. Concretely, x,θ∈ℝnx,\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and

pθ​(x)=N⁡(x∣θ,σ2​𝐈),\displaystyle p_{\theta}(x)=N\left({x}\mid{\theta},{\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}}\right), (5.1)

for some given σ>0\sigma>0. We also assume that ψ=(θ¯,Σ)\psi=(\bar{\theta},\Sigma) and

qψ​(θ)=N⁡(θ∣θ¯,Σ),\displaystyle q_{\psi}(\theta)=N\left({\theta}\mid{\bar{\theta}},{\Sigma}\right), (5.2)

where Σ\Sigma is a covariance matrix. Then,

ℙF​(x)=N⁡(x∣θ¯,Σ+σ2​𝐈),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)=N\left({x}\mid{\bar{\theta}},{\Sigma+\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}}\right), (5.3)

and we can calculate the phenotype gradient estimator analytically:

ℐ​[ℙF​(x)]−1​∂∂θ¯¯p​ℱW=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​(xi−θ¯),\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right]^{-1}\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial{\bar{\theta}}}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))(x_{i}-\bar{\theta}), (5.4)
ℐ​[ℙF​(x)]−1​∂∂Σ¯p​ℱW=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​(xi−θ¯)​(xi−θ¯)⊤−Σ−σ2​𝐈,\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right]^{-1}\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial{\Sigma}}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))(x_{i}-\bar{\theta})(x_{i}-\bar{\theta})^{\top}-\Sigma-\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}, (5.5)

where the Fisher information matrix ℐ​[ℙF​(x)]\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right] is defined by (2.9). The derivation is given in Appendix  C.3.1. This result is similar to the rank-μ\mu update of CMA-ES [1; 19; 37]. When we use the Fisher information matrix for qψ​(θ)q_{\psi}(\theta), we do not have a clear expression as in (5.4). Therefore, in the Gaussian OIU case, it is more practical to use the natural phenotype gradient estimator for ℙF​(x)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x) rather than for qψ​(θ)q_{\psi}(\theta).

5.2 Reinforcement Learning and its Phenotype Gradient Estimator

We next calculate the natural phenotype gradient estimator for RL problem introduced in Section 3.1.2. We first consider a case where the state 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the action 𝒜\mathcal{A} are both discrete. In addition, for simplicity, we fix the initial state x0x_{0}. In this subsection, we take the genotype θ\theta to be the policy π\pi itself. Let j⁡(s′,a,s):=∑t=0T𝕀⁡(st=s′,at=a,st+1=s)j(s^{\prime},a,s):=\sum_{t=0}^{T}\mathbb{I}(s_{t}=s^{\prime},a_{t}=a,s_{t+1}=s) be the empirical count of the transition (s′,a,s)(s^{\prime},a,s) in an observed sequence xx. Also, let j⁡(a,s):=∑t=0T−1𝕀⁡(st=s,at=a)j(a,s):=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{I}(s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a) be the empirical count of the state-action pair (a,s)(a,s) in the observed sequence xx. Then,

pθ​(x)=(∏t=0T−1𝐓⁡(st+1∣st,at))​∏s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜π​(a∣s)j⁡(a,s).\displaystyle p_{\theta}(x)=\left(\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbf{T}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t})\right)\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\mid s)^{j(a,s)}. (5.6)

We introduce a Dirichlet distribution as the conjugate prior qψq_{\psi}:

ψ=(αa,s)a∈𝒜,s∈𝒮,\displaystyle\psi=(\alpha_{a,s})_{a\in\mathcal{A},s\in\mathcal{S}}, (5.7)
qψ(θ)=∏s∈𝒮Dir(𝝅(⋅∣s)∣(αa,s)a∈𝒜).\displaystyle q_{\psi}(\theta)=\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\mathrm{Dir}(\bm{\pi}(\cdot\mid s)\mid(\alpha_{a,s})_{a\in\mathcal{A}}). (5.8)

Let jij_{i} be the empirical count of the transition in the ii-th trial. The phenotype gradient estimator is given by

∂∂αa,s¯p​ℱW=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​[(∑l=0ji​(a,s)−11l+αa,s)−(∑l=0∑a′∈𝒜ji​(a′,s)−11l+∑a′∈𝒜αa′,s)].\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial{\alpha_{a,s}}}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\left[\left(\sum_{l=0}^{j_{i}(a,s)-1}\frac{1}{l+\alpha_{a,s}}\right)-\left(\sum_{l=0}^{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}j_{i}(a^{\prime},s)-1}\frac{1}{l+\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\alpha_{a^{\prime},s}}\right)\right]. (5.9)

The derivation is given in Section C.3.3.

5.3 Application of Reparameterization Trick to RL

When the states and actions are continuous, we need to utilize the reparameterization trick to approximate the phenotype gradient estimator. In contrast to Section 5.2, here we take the genotype θ\theta to be logit of the policy:

θ\displaystyle\theta :=(θa,s)a∈𝒜,s∈𝒮,\displaystyle:=(\theta_{a,s})_{a\in\mathcal{A},s\in\mathcal{S}}, (5.10)
πθ​(a∣s)\displaystyle\qquad\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) =exp⁡(θa,s)∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(θa′,s).\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(\theta_{a,s})}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\exp(\theta_{a^{\prime},s})}. (5.11)

We assume the ZOO setting where the population is Gaussian. Concretely, we assume

θ=βψ​(ξ):=θ¯+σ​ξ,\displaystyle\theta=\beta_{\psi}(\xi):=\bar{\theta}+\sigma\xi, (5.12)
ξ∼N⁡(ξ∣𝟎,𝐈),\displaystyle\xi\sim N\left({\xi}\mid{\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}}\right), (5.13)

where σ>0\sigma>0 is a fixed hyperparameter and θ¯\bar{\theta} is the parameter to be optimized. We identify θ¯\bar{\theta} with ψ\psi in the following discussion.

Let us compute the reparameterized gradient estimator (4.36). We decompose the empirical count j⁡(a,s):=∑t=0T−1𝕀⁡(st=s,at=a)j(a,s):=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{I}(s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a) as j⁡(a,s)=j⁡(s)​j​(a∣s)j(a,s)=j(s)j(a\mid s), where j⁡(s)=∑a∈𝒜j⁡(a,s)j(s)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}j(a,s) is the empirical count of the state ss and j⁡(a∣s)=j⁡(a,s)/j⁡(s)j(a\mid s)=j(a,s)/j(s) is the empirical conditional distribution of the action aa given the state ss. Then, the reparameterized gradient estimator (4.36) is given by

∂∂ψ¯a,sr​ℱW=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​[j⁡(a,s)−j⁡(s)​πβψ​(ξ)​(a∣s)].\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{r}}_{a,s}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\left[j(a,s)-j(s)\pi_{\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}(a\mid s)\right]. (5.14)

The derivation is given in Section C.3.4. This update rule resembles ancestral reinforcement learning [33] in that a descendant generation tends to repeat the action of its ancestors with higher cumulative rewards.

This estimator is not an exact Rao-Blackwellization, since it contains ξ\xi. Yet, the dependency on ξ\xi is very weak when σ\sigma is small. This fact is verified by the Taylor expansion of πβψ​(ξ)​(a∣s)\pi_{\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}(a\mid s) around θ=βψ​(ξ)\theta=\beta_{\psi}(\xi):

πβψ​(ξ)​(a∣s)\displaystyle\pi_{\beta_{\psi}(\xi)}(a\mid s) =πθ¯(a∣s)+[diag(𝝅θ¯(⋅∣s))−𝝅θ¯(⋅∣s)𝝅θ¯(⋅∣s)⊤]σξ+O(∥σξ∥2)\displaystyle=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(a\mid s)+\left[\mathrm{diag}(\bm{\pi}_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid s))-\bm{\pi}_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid s)\bm{\pi}_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid s)^{\top}\right]\sigma\xi+O(\|\sigma\xi\|^{2}) (5.15)
=πθ¯​(a∣s)+O⁡(‖σ​ξ‖).\displaystyle=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(a\mid s)+O(\|\sigma\xi\|). (5.16)

Substituting this expansion into (5.14), we obtain

∂∂ψ¯a,sr​ℱW\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}}^{\mathrm{r}}_{a,s}\mathcal{F}_{W} =1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​[j⁡(a,s)−j⁡(s)​(πθ¯​(a∣s)+O⁡(‖σ​ξ‖))]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\left[j(a,s)-j(s)\left(\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(a\mid s)+O(\|\sigma\xi\|)\right)\right]
=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​[j⁡(a,s)−j⁡(s)​πθ¯​(a∣s)]⏟independent of ​ξ+O⁡(‖σ​ξ‖).\displaystyle=\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\left[j(a,s)-j(s)\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(a\mid s)\right]}_{\text{independent of }\xi}+O(\|\sigma\xi\|). (5.17)

The leading term is independent of ξ\xi and thus Rao-Blackwellized, while the remaining term is only O⁡(‖σ​ξ‖)O(\|\sigma\xi\|).

6 Numerical Experiments

In this section, we demonstrate the superiority of the phenotype gradient estimator and associated PAES to the conventional genotype gradient estimator and the associated ES by using three classes of problems. We observe that the phenotype gradient estimator consistently outperforms the genotype estimator across all classes tested.

6.1 Gaussian OIU

We first evaluate the performance of ES and PAES on the OIU with the Gaussian distribution problem introduced in Section 5.1.

6.1.1 Setup

The objective function ff is chosen from the BBOB test suite [16]. We note that BBOB benchmarks are minimization problems and, in this section, we use PAES for minimization problems by transforming ff to −f-f. The search space is d=40d=40 dimensional, and the population size is 100100. We run each algorithm for up to 50005000 generations and repeat the experiment with 10 different random seeds. The search space is [−5,5]d[-5,5]^{d} for all functions. The magnitude σ\sigma of the input noise is set to 0.10.1. We initialize the population as N⁡(θ∣0,12​𝐈)N\left({\theta}\mid{0},{\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{I}}\right). The population is represented as a Gaussian distribution N(⋅∣θ¯,Σ)N\left({\cdot}\mid{\bar{\theta}},{\Sigma}\right), where both mean θ¯\bar{\theta} and covariance matrix Σ\Sigma are updated. We utilized the vanilla SGD with learning rate 0.010.01 for both ES and PAES. For the weighting function WW, we use a rank-based linear function commonly used in CMA-ES [19]. Let rank⁡(xi)∈{1,…,N}\mathrm{rank}(x_{i})\in\{1,\ldots,N\} be the rank of xix_{i} when the population is sorted by F⁡(xi)F(x_{i}) in descending order. Let p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1] be a hyperparameter that specifies the fraction of the population to receive a nonzero weight, and define ξ:=⌊p​N⌋\xi:=\lfloor pN\rfloor as the number of selected individuals. We set p=0.8p=0.8 (hence ξ=80\xi=80 for N=100N=100) and define

W⁡(F⁡(xi))={wmax⋅ξ−rank⁡(xi)ξ−1rank⁡(xi)≤ξ,0rank⁡(xi)>ξ,\displaystyle W(F(x_{i}))=\begin{cases}w_{\max}\cdot\dfrac{\xi-\mathrm{rank}(x_{i})}{\xi-1}&\mathrm{rank}(x_{i})\leq\xi,\\ 0&\mathrm{rank}(x_{i})>\xi,\end{cases} (6.1)

where wmax=0.1w_{\max}=0.1. For ES, we estimate the gradient via rank-μ\mu CMA-ES [19] as

∂∂θ¯​ℱW=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(F⁡(xi))​(θi−θ¯),\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{\theta}}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(F(x_{i}))\left(\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta}\right), (6.2)
∂∂Σ​ℱW=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(F⁡(xi))​((θi−θ¯)​(θi−θ¯)⊤−Σ).\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\Sigma}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(F(x_{i}))\left((\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta})(\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta})^{\top}-\Sigma\right). (6.3)

For PAES, we use the update rule (5.4).

6.1.2 Performance evaluation

Figure 6.1 shows the mean difference between the final objective values and the optimum values for 10 runs of all 24 BBOB functions. The figure indicates that PAES consistently achieves lower errors than ES. Figure 6.2 shows the convergence curves for three representative cases. A typical case is the sphere function (f1) where PAES converges faster than ES and achieves a lower objective value at the end of the optimization. Another case is Schwefel x*sin(x) (f20), where PAES finds a significantly better solution than ES (see also Figure 6.1). This function has many local minima on a scale comparable to the input noise, and thus the genotypic information F⁡(θi)F(\theta_{i}) is obscured by the noise. As a result, ES was unable to find the optimal solution, while PAES found the optimal solution using phenotypic information xix_{i} directly. The last case is the Katsuura function (f23), where both methods failed to minimize the objective function and plateaued at a similar level. The function (f23) has many local minima arranged in a lattice pattern within the input noise scale. The input noise averages such local structures and the objective function F⁡(θ)F(\theta) becomes flat, making it difficult for both ES and PAES to minimize the objective function.

The convergence curves for all 2424 functions are provided in Appendix D. We also note that the computation times for 5000 generations for ES and PAES on all 2424 BBOB functions are comparable (Appendix D).

6.2 Reinforcement Learning (Exact Rao-Blackwellization)

Next, we evaluate the performance of PAES for an RL problem with discrete states and actions where the exact phenotype gradient estimator ( (5.9)) is used.

6.2.1 Setup

We adopt the FrozenLake-v1 environment [50]. The environment consists of 1616 states and 44 actions (left/down/right/up) in a 4×44\times 4 grid world. For ES, we parameterize the policy using a Q-table, each of which is initialized by a normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,0.01)\mathcal{N}(0,0.01). For PAES, we parametrize the policy as a set of Dirichlet distributions, each of which corresponds to a state xx and whose parameter is initialized by αs=(1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0)\alpha_{s}=(1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0). The population size is set to 100100, and we optimize the policy using vanilla SGD with a learning rate 0.010.01 for both ES and PAES. The weighting function WW is defined by using the cumulative reward rir_{i} of each policy in the population as follows:

W⁡(ri)=ri−r¯σ^r,\displaystyle W(r_{i})=\frac{r_{i}-\bar{r}}{\hat{\sigma}_{r}}, (6.4)

where r¯=1N​∑j=1Nrj\bar{r}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}r_{j} and σ^r=1N​∑j=1N(rj−r¯)2\hat{\sigma}_{r}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}(r_{j}-\bar{r})^{2}}.

6.2.2 Performance evaluation

Since the performance of ES and PAES may depend on the hyperparameters σ\sigma and S=∑a∈𝒜αa,sS=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\alpha_{a,s} respectively, we ran each algorithm with different random seeds and hyperparameters. We measure the performance of the algorithm at each step by the cumulative reward of the updated policy, which is obtained by normalizing the parameters αs\alpha_{s} of the Dirichlet distribution for PAES and directly from the Q-table for ES. This evaluation of the reward is different from the evaluation of the cumulative rewards in the population in that we make the policy deterministic by taking the action with highest probability for each state. Figure 6.3 (a) shows the learning curves of each algorithm for the best hyperparameter setting, where the vertical axis shows the cumulative reward of the updated policy. Here, we choose the best hyperparameter setting for each algorithm by the speed of convergence of the cumulative reward and stability of the learning curve (see Appendix E.1 for details). Although we run the experiment until 500500 generations, we show only the first 250250 generations for better visibility. PAES converges to a high cumulative reward of the updated policy faster than ES. Figure 6.3 (b,c) shows the sensitivity of the cumulative reward of the updated policy at the last 5050 generations to the hyperparameters. We observe that the performance of ES is better when the σ\sigma is no less than 0.10.1, which means that the variance of the population is large. On the other hand, the performance of PAES is better when SS is smaller than 11, which means that the variance of the population is large like ES. The comparison of computation time is provided in Appendix E.2, where PAES converges faster than ES in terms of wall-clock time as well.

6.3 Reinforcement Learning (Reparameterization Trick Approximation)

We evaluate the performance of PAES for more complex RL tasks by applying the reparameterization trick approximation of the phenotype gradient estimator (5.14). In the following, we present learning curves in terms of generations. The comparison of computation time is provided in Appendix E.2, where the learning curves are similar to those in the main text.

6.3.1 CartPole

We apply the approximated PAES with reparameterization trick to the CartPole-v1 environment [50]. We note that the PAES with the exact Rao-Blackwellization  (5.9) is not applicable to this environment because the state space is continuous. The maximum step for each episode is set to 500500, which is equal to the maximum reward for each episode. We introduce early stopping when the mean reward of the population reaches 475475. The policy is represented by a three-layer neural network with 3232 hidden units with the t​a​n​htanh activation function. The final layer outputs the action probabilities by applying the softmax function. The policy is initialized by the Xavier initialization [14]. We add Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ=0.1\sigma=0.1 to the policy parameters. The population size is set to 100100. We optimize the policy by Adam with learning rate 0.0010.001, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999 for both ES and PAES. We define the weighting function WW by using the cumulative reward rir_{i} of each policy in the population as follows:

W⁡(ri)=rank⁡(ri)N−1−12,\displaystyle W(r_{i})=\frac{\mathrm{rank}(r_{i})}{N-1}-\frac{1}{2}, (6.5)

where rank⁡(ri)∈{0,1,…,N−1}\mathrm{rank}(r_{i})\in\{0,1,\ldots,N{-}1\} is the zero-indexed rank of rir_{i} among {r1,…,rN}\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{N}\}. This weighting function is commonly used in the application of ES to RL problems [44]. For ES, we use antithetic sampling, which is a common variance reduction technique for ES [44]. To apply the update rule of PAES (5.14), we collect the empirical count j⁡(a,s)j(a,s) of each policy in the population and then compute the gradient of the original policy by back-propagating the gradient  (5.14) to the network.

Figure 6.4 shows the learning curves of ES and PAES for CartPole-v1. PAES converges significantly faster than ES in terms of the number of generations, which demonstrates the effectiveness of PAES with the reparameterization trick in RL problems.

6.3.2 Pendulum

Next, we evaluate the performance of PAES for the Pendulum-v1 environment [50], where both state and action spaces are continuous. The policy is represented by a three-layer MLP with 6464 hidden units with the t​a​n​htanh activation function, which directly outputs the continuous action. When we generate a population in both ES and PAES, the policy parameters θ\theta are perturbed by Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ\sigma. Here, the value of σ\sigma starts from 0.050.05 and linearly decays to 0.010.01 over 30003000 generations. In addition, for PAES, we add Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ\sigma to the action output of the policy. This noise corresponds to the phenotypic noise in PAES and accelerates exploration in the action space. For ES, we found that adding noise to the action worsens the performance (results not shown), and thus we show the result without adding noise to actions. We set the threshold for early stopping to −200-200. The other settings are the same as those in CartPole-v1.

Figure 6.4 (b) shows the learning curves of ES and PAES. The vertical axis shows the deterministic reward of the updated policy, which is evaluated by not adding the action noise to the policy. The result shows that PAES converges faster than ES in terms of generations.

6.3.3 Swimmer

Finally, we evaluate the performance of PAES in the Swimmer-v5 environment [50], which is a more complex continuous control environment. The setting is the same as those in Pendulum-v1, except for the following points. The standard deviation σ\sigma of the noise added to policies t​h​e​t​atheta and actions starts from 0.20.2 and linearly decays to 0.050.05 over 50005000 generations. We added larger noise because, with smaller noise starting from σ=0.05\sigma=0.05, both ES and PAES failed to find a successful policy within 50005000 generations for about half of the seeds. This is reasonable because the Swimmer environment is known to have many local minima, and thus exploration is necessary to find the successful policy. We balance exploration and stability after convergence by tuning the standard deviation σ\sigma of the noise.

Figure 6.4 (c) shows the learning curves of ES and PAES for Swimmer-v5. PAES converges faster than ES in terms of generations, demonstrating that phenotypic information can also accelerate learning in complex continuous control environments.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we have investigated the question of whether the realization of the input is useful to accelerate the ES in OIU problems. We showed that the acceleration of the ES is achieved by PAES in which the phenotype gradient estimator utilizes the information of input realization, i.e., phenotype information. Then, we generalized this result by clarifying that the acceleration is achieved by Rao-Blackwellization, which reduces the variance of the gradient estimation by utilizing the realization of the input. We also provide both analytical forms and an approximation of the phenotype gradient estimator in PAES to cover a variety of problems. Numerical experiments demonstrated the superiority of PAES, which is consistent with our theoretical results. PAES achieves faster convergence than ES from simple optimization to more complex RL benchmarks. We found that the computation time of PAES is comparable to that of ES, which means that PAES is more efficient than ES even in terms of wall-clock time. Furthermore, to obtain finer gradient estimators, PAES could be combined with several other techniques for RL, such as the baseline control [15].

A limitation of PAES is that it requires the input distribution to be in some well-behaved class to calculate the phenotype gradient analytically. To apply PAES to a broader class of problems, we need to develop an approximation method for the phenotype gradient estimator. A possible approach is to use the phenotypic information to imitate the input xx with a higher objective value in the population. Indeed, the phenotype gradient estimator for the Gaussian OIU problem (5.4) can be interpreted as imitating the input xx with a higher objective value in the population. In addition, the reparameterization trick (5.14) employed for RL can be regarded as imitating the action of agents with a higher reward in the population. These results indicate that imitation of the ancestors with a higher objective value in the population can accelerate the ES, even though it may not necessarily be represented as Rao-Blackwellization.

The application of OIU has been expanding from classical examples of manufacturing to robotics and RL. Another application of OIU would be Large Language Models, in which the stochastic output is guided by optimizing prompts and context information fed to LLM. This expansion indicates possible broad applications of this paper. Moreover, there are several solutions to OIU: ES, gradient-based methods, and Bayesian optimization. Although we focused only on ES and its extension PAES, a similar idea may be applicable to other solutions. For such directions, the observation that Rao-Blackwellization via the realization of the input resembles imitation learning might be useful to construct improved algorithms.

Appendix A Related Work to OIU and PAES

ES [41] is applied to a broad class of problems, especially when the gradient of the objective function is not available. ES represents the population as a probability distribution and aims to maximize the expected value of the objective function over population. The expected value is maximized via the stochastic gradient ascent, where the gradient is estimated by using the samples of objective values in the population. Variants of ES, such as CMA-ES [19; 18], Natural Evolution Strategy (NES) [52], and Information Geometric Optimization (IGO) [37] are widely applied to various problems and have high performance on benchmark functions [17; 43]. In the context of black-box optimization, ES is also called zeroth-order optimization (ZOO), and its properties such as convergence rate and sample complexity have been studied [35; 11; 47; 10; 55]. In this paper, we improve ES for OIU by tapping into the information of realized input xx.

Variance reduction techniques for gradient estimation have been studied in various contexts of machine learning. One technique is Rao-Blackwellization, in which we can reduce the variance of estimator by taking conditional expectation with respect to irrelevant variable. Rao-Blackwellization is applied to variational inference [45; 39; 26], the estimation of the gradient of discrete variables [56; 29], and the construction of action-dependent baselines for policy gradient methods [53]. Another technique is the reparameterization trick (also known as stochastic backpropagation [42]), which, for a compositional objective function, computes some part of the objective function analytically and then estimates the gradient of the other part by sampling. The reparameterization trick is empirically shown to have a smaller variance [46; 31] and theoretical analysis is provided for some idealized cases [54]. The reparameterization trick is also applied to the variational auto encoder [25], and variational inference [26].

Appendix B Contextual Optimization under Input Uncertainty (COIU)

As an extension of OIU, we also define a Contextual Optimization under Input Uncertainty (COIU). At each trial, we are given a context c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} which is drawn from some distribution ν⁡(c)\nu(c). For each θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, we define a conditional probability distribution pθ​(x∣c)p_{\theta}(x\mid c) on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For a function f:𝒳×𝒞→ℝf\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}, the objective function is given by

F⁡(θ):=𝔼ν⁡(c)​[𝔼pθ​(x∣c)​[f⁡(x,c)]].\displaystyle F(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu(c)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(x\mid c)}\left[{f(x,c)}\right]}\right]. (B.1)

B.1 Examples of the Problem

B.1.1 Mixture of Experts

Let us consider a classification problem. We are given a context cc that follows a distribution ν⁡(c)\nu(c), and we need to output the corresponding label in a discrete set 𝒳\mathcal{X}. The loss function is f⁡(c,x)f(c,x). One solution to this classification problem is MoE. Assume that we have a set of experts ϕ={ϕi}i=1k\phi=\{\phi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}, each of which defines a distribution πϕi​(x∣c)\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c) over the output labels. In MoE, we first choose an expert ii with probability α⁡(i∣c,ρ)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho), where ρ\rho is a parameter. Then, the chosen expert outputs a label with probability πϕi​(x∣c)\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c). Our aim is to optimize each experts ϕ\phi and the choice rule ρ\rho of experts to minimize the expected loss. The expected loss when we choose the ii-th expert is given by

F⁡(i)=𝔼ν⁡(c)​[𝔼πθi​(x∣c)​[f⁡(c,x)]].\displaystyle F(i)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu(c)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta_{i}}(x\mid c)}\left[{f(c,x)}\right]}\right]. (B.2)

Therefore, the optimization of ϕi\phi_{i} is formulated in the framework of (B.1). The expected loss when we choose exert stochastically from α⁡(i∣c,ρ)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho) is

F⁡(ϕ,ρ)=𝔼ν⁡(c)​[𝔼πθi​(x∣c)​α​(i∣c,ρ)​[f⁡(c,x)]].\displaystyle F(\phi,\rho)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu(c)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta_{i}}(x\mid c)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho)}\left[{f(c,x)}\right]}\right]. (B.3)

In Section B.2.1, we will solve MoE by ES and see that α⁡(i∣c,ρ)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho) corresponds to a population distribution of ES and the expected loss to ℱ\mathcal{F} in (2.3).

B.1.2 Classification with Bandit Feedback

We consider a classification problem with bandit feedback [24]. The classification problem is the same setting as the previous subsection. We note that this setting is different from the usual classification problems in that we do not know the correct class for cc. Suppose that we have a stochastic classification algorithm πθ​(x∣c)\pi_{\theta}(x\mid c), which is a conditional probability distribution on 𝒳\mathcal{X} given cc. The expected loss is given by

F⁡(θ)=𝔼ν⁡(c)​[𝔼πθ​(x∣c)​[f⁡(c,x)]].\displaystyle F(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu(c)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(x\mid c)}\left[{f(c,x)}\right]}\right]. (B.4)

By setting

pθ​(x)=πθ​(x∣c),\displaystyle p_{\theta}(x)=\pi_{\theta}(x\mid c), (B.5)

the expected value of the feedback is formulated in the framework of COIU (B.1).

B.2 Phenotype gradient estimators for COIU

We derive phenotype gradient estimators for COI in thie section for the two examples we introduced above.

B.2.1 Mixture of Experts

We consider the example in Section B.1.1. Let us denote the event that the ii-th expert with parameter ϕi\phi_{i} is chosen by θi,ϕi\theta_{i,\phi_{i}}. Also, let ψ=(ϕ,ρ)\psi=(\phi,\rho). We also define

qψ​(θi,ϕi∣c)=δϕi​(θi,ϕi)​α​(i∣c,ρ),\displaystyle q_{\psi}(\theta_{i,\phi_{i}}\mid c)=\delta_{\phi_{i}}(\theta_{i,\phi_{i}})\alpha(i\mid c,\rho), (B.6)
pθi,ϕi​(x∣c)=πϕi​(x∣c),\displaystyle p_{\theta_{i,\phi_{i}}}(x\mid c)=\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c), (B.7)

where δ\delta is the delta function. Under this setting, the expected loss (B.3) can be written as

F⁡(ϕ,ρ)=𝔼ν⁡(c)​[𝔼qψ​(θi,ϕi)​[𝔼pθi,ϕi​(x∣c)​[f⁡(x,c)]]]=ℱ⁡(ψ).\displaystyle F(\phi,\rho)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu(c)}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta_{i,\phi_{i}})}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{i,\phi_{i}}(x\mid c)}}\left[{f(x,c)}\right]}\right]}\right]=\mathcal{F}(\psi). (B.8)

Therefore, MoE is formulated as smoothed objective function of COIU (cf. (4.1)).

From this observation, we can calculate the phenotype gradient estimator for MoE. We know that

ℙF(x,θi,ϕi∣c,ψ)=πϕi(x∣c)α(i∣c,ρ),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x,\theta_{i,\phi_{i}}\mid c,\psi)=\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho), (B.9)
ℙF​(x∣c,ψ)=∑i=1kπϕi​(x∣c)​α​(i∣c,ρ).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x\mid c,\psi)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho). (B.10)

We also know that

ℙF​(θi,ϕi∣c,x,ψ)=πϕi​(x∣c)​α​(i∣c,ρ)∑i=1kπϕi​(x∣c)​α​(i∣c,ρ).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta_{i,\phi_{i}}\mid c,x,\psi)=\frac{\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho)}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho)}. (B.11)

Therefore, the phenotype gradient estimator is given by

∂∂ρ¯p​ℱW\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial{\rho}}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W} =1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​∂log⁡ℙF​(x∣c,ψ)∂ρ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x\mid c,\psi)}{\partial\rho} (B.12)
=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​[πϕi​(x∣c)​∂∂ρ​α​(i∣c,ρ)∑i=1kπθi​(x∣c)​α​(i∣c,ρ)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\left[\frac{\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x\mid c)\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\alpha(i\mid c,\rho)}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_{\theta_{i}}(x\mid c)\alpha(i\mid c,\rho)}\right] (B.13)
=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​ℙF​(i∣c,x,ρ)​∂∂ρ​log⁡α⁡(i∣c,ρ).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(i\mid c,x,\rho)\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\log\alpha(i\mid c,\rho). (B.14)

Also, we have

∂∂ϕi¯p​ℱW\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial{\phi_{i}}}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W} =1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​∂log⁡ℙF​(x∣c,ψ)∂ϕi\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x\mid c,\psi)}{\partial\phi_{i}} (B.15)
=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​[α⁡(i∣ci,ρ)​∂∂ϕi​πϕi​(xi∣ci)∑i=1kπθi​(xi∣ci)​α​(i∣ci,ρ)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\left[\frac{\alpha(i\mid c_{i},\rho)\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi_{i}}\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x_{i}\mid c_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_{\theta_{i}}(x_{i}\mid c_{i})\alpha(i\mid c_{i},\rho)}\right] (B.16)
=1N​∑i=1NW⁡(f⁡(xi))​ℙF​(i∣ci,xi,ρ)​∂∂ϕi​log⁡πϕi​(xi∣ci).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W(f(x_{i}))\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(i\mid c_{i},x_{i},\rho)\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi_{i}}\log\pi_{\phi_{i}}(x_{i}\mid c_{i}). (B.17)

These equations resembles the update rule of EM algorithm for MoE [23] in that it utilizes a posterior distribution ℙF​(i∣c,x,ψ)\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(i\mid c,x,\psi) to update the parameter ψ\psi.

B.2.2 Classification with Bandit Feedback

We next consider the example in Section B.1.2. We take the genotype θ\theta to be the classification probability itself. Also, we take a conjugate prior qψq_{\psi} to the multinomial distribution π(⋅∣c)\pi(\cdot\mid c) for each c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} as

qψ(θ∣c)=Dir(π(⋅∣c)∣(αx,c)x∈𝒳).\displaystyle q_{\psi}(\theta\mid c)=\mathrm{Dir}(\pi(\cdot\mid c)\mid(\alpha_{x,c})_{x\in\mathcal{X}}). (B.18)

Under this setting, the phenotype gradient estimator is given by

∂∂αx,c¯p​ℱW=1N​∑i=1Nδc,ci​δx,xi​W​(f⁡(xi))​[1αx,c−1∑x′∈𝒳αx′,c].\displaystyle\overline{\frac{\partial}{\partial{\alpha_{x,c}}}}^{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{F}_{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{c,c_{i}}\delta_{x,x_{i}}W(f(x_{i}))\left[\frac{1}{\alpha_{x,c}}-\frac{1}{\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}\alpha_{x^{\prime},c}}\right]. (B.19)

The calculation is given in Section C.3.2.

Appendix C Proofs

C.1 Proofs in Section 4

Proof of Theroem 3 and Theorem 5.

We prove Theorem 5 which includes Theorem 3 as a special case. We first prove (4.16). From the definition of the Rao-Blackwellized estimator, we have

𝔼ℙF​[RB⁡[U]​({xi(t)}i∈[N])]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right)}\right] =𝔼ℙF​[{xi(t)}i∈[N]]​[𝔼ℙF​[{θi(t)}i∈[N]∣{xi(t)}i∈[N]]​[U⁡({θi(t),xi(t)}i∈[N])]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}[\{{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}]}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}[\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}\mid\{{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}]}\left[{U\left({\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right)}\right]}\right] (C.1)
=𝔼ℙF​[U⁡({θi(t),xi(t)}i∈[N])].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{U\left({\{{\theta_{i}}^{(t)},{x_{i}}^{(t)}\}_{i\in[N]}}\right)}\right]. (C.2)

By the assumption, the right hand side is equal to the gradient of the smoothed objective function.

We next prove (4.17). For notational simplicity, we omit the subscript i∈[N]i\in[N] and the superscript tt indicating the generation in the following equations. Let us define

u:=𝔼ℙF​[U⁡({θi,xi})]=𝔼ℙF​[RB⁡[U]​({xi})].\displaystyle u:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)}\right]. (C.3)

By direct calculation, we have

𝕍ℙF​[U⁡({θi,xi})]\displaystyle\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)\right] (C.4)
=𝔼ℙF​[(U⁡({θi,xi})−u)2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-u\right)^{2}}\right] (C.5)
=𝔼ℙF​[[(U⁡({θi,xi})−RB⁡[U]​({xi}))+(RB⁡[U]​({xi})−u)]2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left[\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right)+\left(\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)-u\right)\right]^{2}}\right] (C.6)
=𝔼ℙF​[(U⁡({θi,xi})−RB⁡[U]​({xi}))2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right)^{2}}\right] (C.7)
+2​𝔼ℙF​[(U⁡({θi,xi})−RB⁡[U]​({xi}))​(RB⁡[U]​({xi})−u)]\displaystyle\quad+2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right)\left(\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)-u\right)}\right] (C.8)
+𝔼ℙF​[(RB⁡[U]​({xi})−u)2]\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left(\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)-u\right)^{2}}\right] (C.9)
=𝔼ℙF​[(U⁡({θi,xi})−RB⁡[U]​({xi}))2]+𝕍ℙF​[RB⁡[U]​({xi})]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right)^{2}}\right]+\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right] (C.10)
+2​𝔼ℙF​[(U⁡({θi,xi})−RB⁡[U]​({xi}))​(RB⁡[U]​({xi})−u)].\displaystyle\quad+2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right)\left(\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)-u\right)}\right]. (C.11)

Since the first term is non-negative, it suffices to show that the last term is zero. This is shown by the following calculation:

𝔼ℙF​[(U⁡({θi,xi})−RB⁡[U]​({xi}))​(RB⁡[U]​({xi})−u)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}}\left[{\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right)\left(\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)-u\right)}\right] (C.12)
=𝔼ℙF​[{xi}]​[𝔼ℙF​[{θi}∣{xi}]​[(U⁡({θi,xi})−RB⁡[U]​({xi}))​(RB⁡[U]​({xi})−u)]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}[\{x_{i}\}]}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}[\{\theta_{i}\}\mid\{x_{i}\}]}\left[{\left(U\left({\{\theta_{i},x_{i}\}}\right)-\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)\right)\left(\mathrm{RB}\left[{U}\right]\left({\{x_{i}\}}\right)-u\right)}\right]}\right] (C.13)

=0.\displaystyle=0. (C.17)

C.2 Proofs in Section 4.5

We prove (4.23). By direct calculation, we have

ℙF​(x)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x) =h⁡(x)​∫exp⁡[(u⁡(x)+ν​ϕ)⋅θ−(ν+1)​A​(θ)−B⁡(ϕ,ν)]​𝑑θ\displaystyle=h(x)\int\exp\left[\left(u(x)+\nu\phi\right)\cdot\theta-(\nu+1)A(\theta)-B(\phi,\nu)\right]\mathrm{d}\theta (C.27)
=h⁡(x)​∫exp⁡[ν′​ϕ′⋅θ−ν′​A​(θ)−B⁡(ϕ,ν)]​𝑑θ.\displaystyle=h(x)\int\exp\left[\nu^{\prime}\phi^{\prime}\cdot\theta-\nu^{\prime}A(\theta)-B(\phi,\nu)\right]\mathrm{d}\theta. (C.28)

By using the definition of the normalization constant B⁡(ϕ,ν)B(\phi,\nu), we have

B(ϕ′,ν′)=log∫exp[ν′ϕ′⋅θ−ν′A(θ)]dθ.\displaystyle B(\phi^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})=\log\int\exp\left[\nu^{\prime}\phi^{\prime}\cdot\theta-\nu^{\prime}A(\theta)\right]\mathrm{d}\theta. (C.29)

Therefore, we have

ℙF​(x)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x) =h⁡(x)​exp⁡[B⁡(ϕ′,ν′)−B⁡(ϕ,ν)],\displaystyle=h(x)\exp\left[B(\phi^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})-B(\phi,\nu)\right], (C.30)

By using this result, we have

∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂ψ\displaystyle\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\psi} =∂∂ψ​[B⁡(ϕ′,ν′)−B⁡(ϕ,ν)].\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi}\left[B(\phi^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})-B(\phi,\nu)\right]. (C.31)

By using the following property of the normalization constant B⁡(ϕ,ν)B(\phi,\nu) [2],

∂B⁡(ϕ,ν)∂ϕ=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ν​θ],\displaystyle\frac{\partial B(\phi,\nu)}{\partial\phi}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\nu\theta}\right], (C.32)
∂B⁡(ϕ,ν)∂ν=𝔼qψ​(θ)​[ϕ⋅θ−A⁡(θ)],\displaystyle\frac{\partial B(\phi,\nu)}{\partial\nu}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\psi}(\theta)}\left[{\phi\cdot\theta-A(\theta)}\right], (C.33)

we have (4.23).

C.3 Proofs in Section 5

C.3.1 Proof of Subsection 5.1

We prove Equation (5.4). As shown in [37; 1; 13], we have

ℐ​[ℙF​(x)]−1​∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂θ¯=(x−θ¯),\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right]^{-1}\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial\bar{\theta}}=(x-\bar{\theta}), (C.34)
ℐ​[ℙF​(x)]−1​∂log⁡ℙF​(x)∂(Σ+σ2​𝐈)=(x−θ¯)​(x−θ¯)⊤−Σ−σ2​𝐈.\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right]^{-1}\frac{\partial\log\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}{\partial(\Sigma+\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})}=(x-\bar{\theta})(x-\bar{\theta})^{\top}-\Sigma-\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}. (C.35)

They also showed that the Fisher information matrix ℐ​[ℙF​(x)]\mathcal{I}\left[{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{F}}(x)}\right] is block-diagonal for θ¯\bar{\theta} and Σ+σ2​𝐈\Sigma+\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}. Since ∂(Σ+σ2​𝐈)∂Σ\frac{\partial(\Sigma+\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})}{\partial\Sigma} is identity, the chain rule implies that the Fisher information matrix and the above partial derivatives are invariant when we change the coordinate system from Σ+σ2​𝐈\Sigma+\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I} to Σ\Sigma. Thus, we have (5.4).

Appendix D Additional Results on OIU with Gaussian Noise

We provide the convergence curves for all 24 BBOB functions under Gaussian OIU setting (Section 6) (Figure D.1 and Figure D.2). Each curve is the mean of 10 different random seeds, and the shaded area shows the standard deviation (std). We also provide the computation time for 5000 generations for ES and PAES on all 24 BBOB functions (Figure D.3).

Appendix E Additional Details of Reinforcement Learning Experiments

E.1 Hyperparameter Sensitivity for FrozenLake-v1

We provide the sensitivity of learning curve of FrozenLake-v1 to the hyperparameters σ\sigma for ES and S=∑a∈𝒜αa,sS=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\alpha_{a,s} for PAES. We observe that the speed of convergence of ES is faster when σ\sigma is no less than 0.10.1 (Figure E.1 (a)). The speed of convergence of PAES is faster when SS is smaller than 11, but the final reward decreases when SS is too small (Figure E.1 (b)). Also, the learning curve fluculates after reaching high cumulative reward (≈0.8\approx 0.8) when SS is too small (S<1S<1) (Figure E.1 (b)).

We note that the Fisher information matrix for the Dirichlet distribution depends on SS even though the ratio of αa,s\alpha_{a,s} is fixed. It means that we need to change the learning rate depending on SS or use natural gradient to compare the speed of convergence for different SS more accurately. However, changing the learning rate and using natural gradient obscure the effect of SS on the learning curve. In this paper, we focus on the effect of the hyperparameter SS on the learning curve, and we do not change the learning rate dependending on SS.

E.2 Computation Time for Reinforcement Learning Experiments

We provide the computation time comparison for the RL experiments in Section 6.2 and Section 6.3.
